naturally.simple: In a way that happens by itself, without people forcing it.
naturally.detailed: In a manner that follows ordinary processes in living systems or the physical world, rather than by artificial interference.
naturally.example: In the creek investigation, crystals formed naturally as the salty water dried on the tray.
naturally.basic: The crystals formed by themselves as the water dried.

obviously.simple: In a way that is easy for anyone to see or understand.
obviously.detailed: In a manner that leaves little doubt because the evidence or meaning is immediately clear to a careful reader.
obviously.example: The graph was obviously incomplete because Friday's temperature column was still blank.
obviously.basic: Anyone could see that the graph was missing Friday's temperature.

particularly.simple: Especially; more than usual, or more than the other things in a group.
particularly.detailed: To a greater degree than in other cases; used to single out one person, place, or idea as more important or more true.
particularly.example: The marker praised Oliver's conclusion, particularly the way he linked each claim to a measurement.
particularly.basic: The marker especially liked the way he linked each claim to a measurement.

previously.simple: At an earlier time; before the moment you are talking about.
previously.detailed: During a time before the event under discussion, often used to compare an earlier result, rule, or situation with the present one.
previously.example: The class compared this year's rainfall with the totals they had previously recorded in Term 1.
previously.basic: They compared this year's rainfall with the totals they had written down earlier.

probably.simple: More likely than not; almost certainly, but not completely proven.
probably.detailed: With a high chance of being true or of happening, while still leaving room for doubt or further evidence.
probably.example: If the soil stays this dry, the seedlings will probably wilt before Friday's lesson.
probably.basic: If the soil stays this dry, the seedlings are likely to wilt before Friday.

rarely.simple: Not often; only on a few occasions, so it stands out when it happens.
rarely.detailed: At unusually long intervals; happening so seldom that it stands out when it does occur.
rarely.example: Frost rarely reaches the coastal plain, so the class treated Tuesday's ice as unusual data.
rarely.basic: Frost almost never reaches the coastal plain.

recently.simple: Not long ago; in the near past rather than years earlier.
recently.detailed: During a short period immediately before the present, used to mark change or new information.
recently.example: The council had recently opened a new wetland walk, so the field notes mentioned fresh boardwalks.
recently.basic: The council had opened a new wetland walk not long ago.

regularly.simple: Again and again on a steady schedule, not just once or twice.
regularly.detailed: At even or frequent intervals, or in a consistent pattern that a reader can rely on.
regularly.example: Oliver watered the seedlings regularly so the results would not be spoiled by uneven care.
regularly.basic: Oliver watered the seedlings on a steady schedule.

slightly.simple: A little; not by a large amount, so the overall picture stays similar.
slightly.detailed: To a small degree; enough to notice, but not enough to change the overall picture completely.
slightly.example: Friday's temperature was slightly higher than Thursday's, but both days stayed in the same band.
slightly.basic: Friday was a bit warmer than Thursday.

suddenly.simple: Quickly and without warning, so there is almost no time to prepare.
suddenly.detailed: Happening in an instant, with little or no time for anyone to prepare or change course.
suddenly.example: The creek rose suddenly after the storm, so the group moved their equipment up the bank.
suddenly.basic: The creek rose very quickly after the storm.

typically.simple: In the usual or expected way for that kind of thing.
typically.detailed: In a manner that matches the common or characteristic pattern, rather than an unusual exception.
typically.example: A Year 6 investigation typically includes a fair test, a results table, and a cautious conclusion.
typically.basic: A Year 6 investigation usually includes a fair test, a table, and a conclusion.

usually.simple: Most of the time; as the ordinary habit or pattern.
usually.detailed: In the majority of cases; according to the ordinary course of events rather than a rare exception.
usually.example: The library is usually quiet after lunch, which is why Oliver drafts his essay there.
usually.basic: The library is quiet after lunch most days.

alloy.simple: A metal made by mixing two or more metals so the new material is more useful.
alloy.detailed: A metallic material formed when metals, and sometimes other elements, are combined so the mixture is stronger, harder, or more workable than the separate parts.
alloy.example: The technology unit compared a soft copper wire with a stronger alloy used in bike frames.
alloy.basic: They compared soft copper with a mixed metal used in bike frames.

altitude.simple: How high a place or aircraft is above sea level.
altitude.detailed: The vertical height of a location, mountain, or aircraft measured from a standard level, usually mean sea level.
altitude.example: The hikers recorded the lookout's altitude so they could explain why the air felt cooler.
altitude.basic: The hikers wrote down how high the lookout was above sea level.

angle.simple: The space between two lines that meet, often measured in degrees.
angle.detailed: The figure formed by two rays that share an endpoint, or the amount of turn between those rays, measured in degrees or radians.
angle.example: They measured the angle of the ramp before predicting how far the toy car would travel.
angle.basic: They measured how steep the ramp was before the test.

axis.simple: An imaginary line that something spins around, or a baseline on a graph.
axis.detailed: A straight reference line about which a body rotates, or a numbered baseline used to locate points on a graph.
axis.example: Earth spins on its axis, which is why we have day and night.
axis.basic: Earth spins around an imaginary line through its middle.

basin.simple: A low area of land that collects water, or the whole area that drains into a river.
basin.detailed: A bowl-shaped hollow in the Earth's surface, or the drainage area whose runoff and groundwater feed one river system.
basin.example: Rain that falls anywhere in the Murray–Darling basin can eventually reach the same river system.
basin.basic: Rain that falls across that huge low area can end up in the same river system.

bedrock.simple: The solid rock that lies underneath the soil.
bedrock.detailed: The hard, unbroken rock layer beneath soil, sand, or loose sediment; it is the foundation on which the landscape sits.
bedrock.example: The creek had cut down to bedrock, so the students could see the original rock instead of only soil.
bedrock.basic: The creek had cut down to the solid rock under the soil.

biomass.simple: The total mass of living things in an area, or plant material used as fuel.
biomass.detailed: The amount of living or recently living organic matter in a habitat, often measured as dry weight, and sometimes burned or processed as an energy source.
biomass.example: They estimated the grassland's biomass by drying and weighing sample clumps of grass.
biomass.basic: They estimated how much living plant material was in the grassland.

biome.simple: A huge natural region with its own climate and typical plants and animals, such as desert or rainforest.
biome.detailed: A large-scale ecological community classified by climate and by the plants and animals adapted to live there.
biome.example: Australia's desert biome has plants that store water, unlike the wet tropical forests further north.
biome.basic: Australia's huge dry region has plants that store water.

buoyancy.simple: The upward push of a liquid or gas that can make an object float.
buoyancy.detailed: The upward force a fluid exerts on an object placed in it, equal to the weight of the fluid the object displaces.
buoyancy.example: The plasticine boat floated because its shape increased buoyancy by displacing more water.
buoyancy.basic: The plasticine boat floated because its shape pushed more water aside.

catchment.simple: The area of land from which rainwater flows into a river, dam, or reservoir.
catchment.detailed: A drainage basin whose surface runoff and groundwater feed a particular river or water-storage system; a key idea in Australian water management.
catchment.example: Anything spilled on the school oval can wash into the local creek catchment after heavy rain.
catchment.basic: Anything spilled on the oval can wash into the land that drains to the local creek.

chlorophyll.simple: The green substance in leaves that captures sunlight so a plant can make food.
chlorophyll.detailed: The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis, giving most healthy leaves their colour.
chlorophyll.example: Yellowing leaves often mean the plant is making less chlorophyll and cannot trap sunlight well.
chlorophyll.basic: Yellowing leaves often mean the plant is making less of the green stuff that traps sunlight.

circuit.simple: A complete path that electricity can travel around.
circuit.detailed: A closed loop of conductors and components that allows electric current to flow from a source and return, lighting a globe or running a motor.
circuit.example: The globe stayed dark until Maya closed the circuit with the final crocodile clip.
circuit.basic: The globe stayed dark until Maya finished the electrical path.

combustion.simple: The process of burning a fuel in oxygen to release heat and light.
combustion.detailed: A chemical reaction in which a fuel combines rapidly with oxygen, producing heat, light, and waste gases such as carbon dioxide.
combustion.example: The class listed water and carbon dioxide as products of combustion when the candle burned.
combustion.basic: They listed water and carbon dioxide as what you get when the candle burns.

compound.simple: A substance made when two or more elements join chemically in a fixed way.
compound.detailed: A pure substance whose particles contain atoms of different elements bonded in a definite ratio, so its properties differ from those of the separate elements.
compound.example: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen, not just a loose mix of the two gases.
compound.basic: Water is hydrogen and oxygen joined together, not just mixed.

continent.simple: One of Earth's huge land masses, such as Australia or Asia.
continent.detailed: A very large, continuous area of land, conventionally one of the main global landmasses used on maps and in geography.
continent.example: Australia is both a country and a continent, which is unusual on a world map.
continent.basic: Australia is both a country and one of Earth's huge land masses.

crater.simple: A bowl-shaped hole made by a volcano or by something hitting the ground from space.
crater.detailed: A roughly circular depression formed by volcanic explosion or collapse, or by the impact of a meteorite.
crater.example: The photograph of the Moon showed a crater larger than some Australian towns.
crater.basic: The Moon photo showed a huge bowl-shaped hole.

crystal.simple: A solid whose particles line up in a regular pattern, often with flat, shiny faces.
crystal.detailed: A mineral or chemical solid with an ordered internal lattice that can grow into geometric faces, such as a quartz point or a salt cube.
crystal.example: As the salty water evaporated, a cube-shaped crystal of salt appeared on the black paper.
crystal.basic: As the salty water dried, a cube of salt appeared on the paper.

delta.simple: Low land built up where a river drops sand and silt as it meets the sea.
delta.detailed: A deposit of sediment, often roughly triangular, formed at a river mouth when the current slows and drops its load.
delta.example: Farms on a river delta are fertile because floods keep adding new silt.
delta.basic: Farms at the river mouth are fertile because floods keep adding new silt.

digestion.simple: The breaking down of food so the body can use the nutrients.
digestion.detailed: The mechanical and chemical process that turns food into smaller nutrients the body can absorb into the blood.
digestion.example: Chewing is the first stage of digestion because it increases the surface area of the food.
digestion.basic: Chewing is the first stage of breaking food down.

eclipse.simple: When one space object blocks the light of another, such as the Moon covering the Sun.
eclipse.detailed: An alignment in which one celestial body passes into another's shadow, or hides another from an observer's view, as when the Sun or Moon is covered.
eclipse.example: During a solar eclipse the Moon slides between Earth and the Sun and the playground goes dim.
eclipse.basic: When the Moon slides between Earth and the Sun, the playground goes dim.

electricity.simple: Energy from moving electric charge, used to power lights, heaters, and machines.
electricity.detailed: A form of energy associated with electric charge, current, and potential difference, found in circuits and in natural events such as lightning.
electricity.example: The wind turbine on the model hill generated enough electricity to light a small globe.
electricity.basic: The model windmill made enough power to light a small globe.

equator.simple: The imaginary line around the middle of Earth, equally far from both poles.
equator.detailed: The great circle at 0° latitude that divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres and marks the hottest general climate band.
equator.example: Towns near the equator stay warm all year because sunlight hits that belt more directly.
equator.basic: Towns near Earth's middle stay warm all year.

estuary.simple: The wide, partly salty mouth of a river where it meets the sea.
estuary.detailed: A coastal water body where freshwater from a river mixes with seawater, often forming a rich habitat for fish, birds, and mangroves.
estuary.example: The class sampled water from the estuary and found it was saltier than the river but fresher than the open sea.
estuary.basic: They sampled water from the river mouth and found it was only partly salty.

extinction.simple: When a whole species dies out and no living members remain.
extinction.detailed: The complete disappearance of a species from Earth, so that breeding populations no longer exist anywhere.
extinction.example: Habitat loss can push a species toward extinction even if a few animals are still alive today.
extinction.basic: Losing habitat can make a whole species die out.

fermentation.simple: A process in which microbes break down sugar without using oxygen, as in bread or yoghurt.
fermentation.detailed: An anaerobic chemical change in which microorganisms convert sugars into acids, gases, or alcohol, used in cooking and some industry.
fermentation.example: Bubbles in the dough showed that fermentation by yeast was producing carbon dioxide.
fermentation.basic: Bubbles in the dough showed that the yeast was breaking down sugar and making gas.

fertiliser.simple: A substance added to soil to give plants extra nutrients so they grow better.
fertiliser.detailed: A natural or manufactured material that supplies nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, or potassium to crops or garden plants.
fertiliser.example: Too much fertiliser washed into the creek and the class linked it to the sudden algal bloom.
fertiliser.basic: Too much plant food washed into the creek and green slime grew quickly.

fibre.simple: Thread-like material in food or plants that helps digestion or makes cloth and ropes strong.
fibre.detailed: Long, thin strands in plant cell walls or animal tissue; the plant material in food that humans do not fully digest, which helps the gut work well.
fibre.example: Wholegrain bread has more fibre than white bread, so it keeps you feeling full for longer.
fibre.basic: Wholegrain bread has more of the plant threads your body does not fully digest.

fungus.simple: A living thing such as a mushroom, mould, or yeast, which is not a plant or an animal.
fungus.detailed: A member of the kingdom of organisms that absorb nutrients from living or dead matter, including mushrooms, moulds, and yeasts.
fungus.example: A fungus on the damp bread released spores that looked like fine dust under the microscope.
fungus.basic: A mould on the damp bread released tiny dust-like spores.

galaxy.simple: A huge group of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity, such as the Milky Way.
galaxy.detailed: A gravitationally bound system of stars, stellar remnants, gas, dust, and dark matter, of which the Milky Way is one example.
galaxy.example: On a dark country night you can see the Milky Way galaxy as a pale band across the sky.
galaxy.basic: On a dark country night you can see our huge star-group as a pale band.

germination.simple: The moment a seed starts to grow into a young plant.
germination.detailed: The process in which a seed or spore begins to develop after taking in water and meeting the right temperature and air conditions.
germination.example: They compared germination in the dark cupboard with seeds left on the sunny windowsill.
germination.basic: They compared which seeds started growing in the dark and which started on the windowsill.

greenhouse.simple: A glass or plastic building that traps heat so plants can grow, or the warming of Earth when gases trap heat.
greenhouse.detailed: A structure with transparent walls that admits sunlight and holds warmth for plants; also used of the atmospheric effect in which certain gases keep Earth warmer.
greenhouse.example: Tomato seedlings in the school greenhouse grew faster because the plastic trapped warm air.
greenhouse.basic: Tomato seedlings in the glass growing-house grew faster because the air stayed warm.

groundwater.simple: Water stored in rocks and soil under the ground.
groundwater.detailed: Fresh water that occupies pores and cracks beneath the Earth's surface and feeds wells, springs, and the base flow of rivers.
groundwater.example: The farmer's well went dry when the groundwater level dropped after three dry summers.
groundwater.basic: The well went dry when the water stored under the ground dropped.

herbivore.simple: An animal that eats only plants, such as grass, leaves, or fruit.
herbivore.detailed: A consumer whose diet consists of plant material rather than other animals, such as a kangaroo grazing on grass.
herbivore.example: A koala is a herbivore that specialises in eucalyptus leaves.
herbivore.basic: A koala is a plant-eater that lives on eucalyptus leaves.

humidity.simple: How much water vapour is in the air, from dry to sticky-wet.
humidity.detailed: The amount of water vapour present in the atmosphere, often given as a percentage of the maximum the air can hold at that temperature.
humidity.example: The data logger showed high humidity after rain, which matched the sticky feeling in the classroom.
humidity.basic: The logger showed the air was very moist after rain.

irrigation.simple: Supplying water to crops through channels, pipes, or sprinklers when rain is not enough.
irrigation.detailed: The planned delivery of water to farmland so plants can grow well in dry weather; a major feature of Australian agriculture.
irrigation.example: Drip irrigation wasted less water than spraying the whole paddock on a windy afternoon.
irrigation.basic: Drip watering wasted less water than spraying the whole paddock.

kinetic.simple: Relating to movement, especially the energy something has because it is moving.
kinetic.detailed: Describing energy or properties that come from motion, as in movement energy, which increases with mass and speed.
kinetic.example: The marble had more kinetic energy at the bottom of the ramp than at the top.
kinetic.basic: The marble had more movement energy at the bottom of the ramp.

limestone.simple: A rock made mainly from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures, used in buildings and cement.
limestone.detailed: A sedimentary rock composed largely of calcium carbonate, often formed from marine fossils and later used as a building stone.
limestone.example: Acid rain had eaten tiny pits in the limestone wall of the old church.
limestone.basic: Acid rain had eaten tiny pits in the pale shell-rock wall.

magnetism.simple: The force that makes magnets attract or repel some metals.
magnetism.detailed: The set of forces and fields produced by magnetic materials or moving electric charges, causing attraction or repulsion.
magnetism.example: They mapped the magnetism of a bar magnet by sprinkling iron filings around it.
magnetism.basic: They mapped the pull of a bar magnet by sprinkling iron filings around it.

mantle.simple: The thick, hot rock layer of Earth between the thin crust and the core.
mantle.detailed: The broad zone of solid but slowly flowing silicate rock that lies beneath Earth's crust and surrounds the core.
mantle.example: Slow movement in the mantle drags the tectonic plates that sit on Earth's crust.
mantle.basic: Slow movement in the hot rock under the crust drags the plates.

metamorphic.simple: Describes rock that has been changed by heat and pressure deep underground.
metamorphic.detailed: Formed when existing rock is transformed in texture or mineral make-up without fully melting, typically under high heat and pressure.
metamorphic.example: Slate is a metamorphic rock that began as mudstone and was squeezed and heated.
metamorphic.basic: Slate is a rock that began as mudstone and was changed by heat and pressure.

mineral.simple: A natural solid from the Earth with a definite chemical make-up, such as quartz or salt.
mineral.detailed: A naturally occurring inorganic solid with an ordered structure and a characteristic chemical composition.
mineral.example: Quartz is a mineral you can identify by its hardness and glassy faces.
mineral.basic: Quartz is a natural solid you can identify by its hardness and glassy faces.

nucleus.simple: The control centre of a cell, or the tiny dense centre of an atom.
nucleus.detailed: The membrane-bound structure that holds a cell's genetic material; also the dense core of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
nucleus.example: Under the microscope the stained nucleus looked like a dark round spot inside each cell.
nucleus.basic: Under the microscope the cell's control centre looked like a dark round spot.

omnivore.simple: An animal that eats both plants and other animals.
omnivore.detailed: A consumer whose diet includes both plant and animal matter, such as a human, a magpie, or a bear.
omnivore.example: A magpie is an omnivore because it takes insects as well as leftover sandwiches.
omnivore.basic: A magpie eats both insects and leftover sandwiches.

orbit.simple: The curved path one object follows around another in space.
orbit.detailed: The regular, usually elliptical path of a planet, moon, or satellite around a more massive body under gravity.
orbit.example: Earth's orbit around the Sun takes about 365 days and gives us a year.
orbit.basic: Earth's path around the Sun takes about 365 days.

ozone.simple: A form of oxygen high in the atmosphere that screens out some harmful sunlight.
ozone.detailed: A molecule of three oxygen atoms (O₃) that forms a layer in the stratosphere and absorbs much ultraviolet radiation.
ozone.example: The class read that the ozone layer over Antarctica thins in spring, letting more ultraviolet light through.
ozone.basic: They read that the high oxygen shield over Antarctica thins in spring.

peninsula.simple: Land that is almost an island, with water on most sides but still joined to the mainland.
peninsula.detailed: A piece of land projecting into a sea or lake and surrounded by water on three sides, such as the Mornington coast near Melbourne.
peninsula.example: Holiday traffic crawls onto the peninsula every summer because there is only one main road in.
peninsula.basic: Holiday traffic crawls onto that almost-island every summer.

pollen.simple: Fine powder from flowers that helps plants make seeds.
pollen.detailed: The tiny grains produced by the male parts of a flower or cone, which carry the cells needed for fertilisation.
pollen.example: Yellow pollen stuck to the bee's legs as it moved from one blossom to the next.
pollen.basic: Yellow flower powder stuck to the bee's legs.

precipitation.simple: Water that falls from the sky as rain, hail, snow, or sleet.
precipitation.detailed: Any form of water, liquid or solid, that condenses in the atmosphere and reaches the ground; a key measurement in climate graphs.
precipitation.example: The climate graph showed almost no precipitation in January, which matched the town's dry summers.
precipitation.basic: The climate graph showed almost no rain in January.

protein.simple: A nutrient in foods such as meat, eggs, and beans that the body uses to build and repair itself.
protein.detailed: A large molecule made of amino acids; essential for growth, enzymes, and the structure of muscles, skin, and many other tissues.
protein.example: The dietitian asked the class to list one protein food they had eaten at breakfast.
protein.basic: She asked them to list one body-building food they had eaten at breakfast.

radiation.simple: Energy that travels as waves or particles, such as light, heat, or X-rays.
radiation.detailed: The emission and travel of energy through space as electromagnetic waves or as streams of particles, including sunlight and medical X-rays.
radiation.example: Dark soil absorbs more solar radiation than pale sand, so it heats up faster at noon.
radiation.basic: Dark soil takes in more of the Sun's energy than pale sand.

rainforest.simple: A thick, wet forest with very high rainfall, such as in tropical Queensland.
rainforest.detailed: A dense forest ecosystem that receives abundant rain and supports layered vegetation and high biodiversity.
rainforest.example: In the Daintree rainforest the canopy is so thick that little sunlight reaches the forest floor.
rainforest.basic: In that thick wet forest the high leaves block most of the sunlight.

refraction.simple: The bending of light when it passes from one material into another.
refraction.detailed: The change in direction of a wave, especially light, as it crosses a boundary between media that it travels through at different speeds.
refraction.example: The pencil looked broken at the waterline because of refraction as light left the water.
refraction.basic: The pencil looked broken at the waterline because the light bent.

respiration.simple: The process living things use to release energy from food, often using oxygen.
respiration.detailed: The set of chemical reactions in cells that break down glucose, usually with oxygen, to release energy the organism can use.
respiration.example: Germinating seeds warmed the flask slightly because respiration releases heat as well as energy.
respiration.basic: The sprouting seeds warmed the flask slightly because they were releasing energy from food.

salinity.simple: How salty a body of water or a patch of soil is.
salinity.detailed: The concentration of dissolved salts in water or soil, a key measure in Australian river, irrigation, and land-care studies.
salinity.example: Rising salinity in the irrigation district left a white crust on the bare paddock.
salinity.basic: Rising saltiness left a white crust on the bare paddock.

satellite.simple: A moon, or a human-made object, that travels around a planet.
satellite.detailed: A natural or artificial body in orbit around a planet or other larger body, used in nature (the Moon) or for communication and weather images.
satellite.example: The weather satellite image showed a cyclone forming off the north-west coast.
satellite.basic: The space-camera picture showed a cyclone forming off the north-west coast.

skeleton.simple: The framework of bones that supports an animal's body.
skeleton.detailed: The internal or external supporting structure of an organism, typically the system of bones in vertebrates that protects organs and allows movement.
skeleton.example: The museum skeleton of a whale showed ribs long enough to walk under.
skeleton.basic: The museum whale bones showed ribs long enough to walk under.

solar.simple: Relating to the Sun, or powered by sunlight.
solar.detailed: Of or produced by the Sun, including sunlight, the Sun's family of planets, and energy collected by sun-powered panels.
solar.example: The school installed solar panels so part of the electricity would come from sunlight.
solar.basic: The school installed sun-powered panels for part of its electricity.

telescope.simple: An instrument that makes distant objects, especially in space, look closer and clearer.
telescope.detailed: An optical or radio device that gathers and focuses electromagnetic radiation so distant celestial objects can be studied.
telescope.example: Through the school telescope Jupiter's four bright moons lined up like tiny beads.
telescope.basic: Through the school star-viewer Jupiter's four bright moons lined up like beads.

tissue.simple: A group of similar cells that work together in a plant or animal, such as muscle.
tissue.detailed: An organised layer or mass of cells that share a structure and function within an organ, for example muscle or leaf cells working together.
tissue.example: Muscle tissue contracts so the arm can bend at the elbow.
tissue.basic: The group of muscle cells contracts so the arm can bend.

tributary.simple: A smaller stream or river that flows into a larger one.
tributary.detailed: A channel that contributes its water to a main river, increasing the main river's flow and extending its catchment.
tributary.example: After the storm every tributary ran brown, and the main river rose by evening.
tributary.basic: After the storm every smaller side-river ran brown.

tsunami.simple: A huge ocean wave caused by an underwater earthquake or landslide.
tsunami.detailed: A series of long-wavelength sea waves generated by a sudden displacement of water, often after a seismic event on the sea floor.
tsunami.example: The coastal town practised a tsunami drill so students knew which hill to climb.
tsunami.basic: The coastal town practised a giant-wave drill so students knew which hill to climb.

turbine.simple: A machine with blades that spin when water, steam, or wind pushes them, often making electricity.
turbine.detailed: A rotary engine that converts the energy of a moving fluid into mechanical work, frequently driving a generator.
turbine.example: Each wind turbine on the ridge turned a generator hidden inside the white tower.
turbine.basic: Each spinning wind-machine on the ridge made electricity inside the tower.

vegetation.simple: The plants growing in a particular place.
vegetation.detailed: The collective plant cover of an area, including trees, shrubs, grasses, and other flora used to describe a landscape.
vegetation.example: After the fire, new vegetation appeared first as green shoots along the blackened trunks.
vegetation.basic: After the fire, new plants appeared first as green shoots.

velocity.simple: Speed in a particular direction, not just how fast something moves.
velocity.detailed: A measure of how fast an object is moving and in which direction; unlike everyday 'speed', it is a vector quantity.
velocity.example: The toy car's velocity increased down the ramp and then dropped when it hit the carpet.
velocity.basic: The toy car went faster down the ramp and then slower on the carpet.

vibration.simple: A rapid back-and-forth shaking that you can often feel or hear.
vibration.detailed: A repeated oscillating movement about a central position, which can travel as a wave through a solid, liquid, or gas.
vibration.example: You could feel the vibration in the desk when the tuning fork touched the wood.
vibration.basic: You could feel the desk shaking when the tuning fork touched the wood.

voltage.simple: The electrical 'push' that makes current flow in a circuit, measured in volts.
voltage.detailed: The electric potential difference between two points, which drives current through a conductor when a circuit is complete.
voltage.example: Two batteries in a line increased the voltage, so the globe shone more brightly.
voltage.basic: Two batteries in a line increased the electrical push, so the globe shone more brightly.

wetland.simple: Land that is wet for much of the year, such as a swamp, marsh, or billabong.
wetland.detailed: An ecosystem where the soil is waterlogged for long periods, supporting plants adapted to wet conditions and providing habitat for many birds and frogs.
wetland.example: Ibis and frogs crowded the wetland after the first autumn rain filled the shallows.
wetland.basic: Ibis and frogs crowded the swampy ground after the first autumn rain.

ambassador.simple: A country's official representative who lives in another country and speaks for their government.
ambassador.detailed: A senior diplomat appointed to represent one nation in another, handling official talks, ceremonies, and the work of an embassy.
ambassador.example: The Australian ambassador in Tokyo explained the new trade agreement to reporters.
ambassador.basic: Australia's top official in Tokyo explained the new trade agreement.

amendment.simple: An official change made to a law, constitution, or written agreement.
amendment.detailed: A formal alteration to a legal or constitutional text, adding, removing, or rewriting a clause after debate and a vote.
amendment.example: Parliament passed an amendment that tightened the rules on plastic packaging.
amendment.basic: Parliament passed a change that tightened the rules on plastic packaging.

archaeology.simple: The study of the past by carefully digging up and examining objects people left behind.
archaeology.detailed: The discipline that recovers and interprets material remains — tools, buildings, bones, and sites — to reconstruct how people lived.
archaeology.example: In the archaeology unit they treated a broken plate as evidence, not as rubbish.
archaeology.basic: In the digs unit they treated a broken plate as evidence.

ballot.simple: A secret vote, or the paper or system used to record that vote.
ballot.detailed: A method of voting, usually private, in which each person marks a paper or machine so choices can be counted fairly.
ballot.example: Each student folded a ballot paper so nobody could see who they had chosen for captain.
ballot.basic: Each student folded a voting paper so nobody could see their choice.

boycott.simple: An organised refusal to buy from, use, or deal with a person, company, or country as a protest.
boycott.detailed: A collective withdrawal of business or participation, used as political or social pressure to force a change in policy or behaviour.
boycott.example: Shoppers organised a boycott of the brand after the report on unfair wages.
boycott.basic: Shoppers refused to buy from the brand after the report on unfair wages.

cabinet.simple: The small group of senior ministers who make the main decisions in a government.
cabinet.detailed: The executive committee of ministers, usually led by a prime minister or premier, that discusses and decides government policy.
cabinet.example: The premier called an emergency cabinet meeting after the flood warning.
cabinet.basic: The premier called an emergency meeting of senior ministers after the flood warning.

capitalism.simple: An economic system in which private people and companies own businesses and try to make a profit.
capitalism.detailed: An economic system based on private ownership of property and firms, market prices, and the pursuit of profit, as distinct from systems where the state owns most industry.
capitalism.example: The HASS lesson compared capitalism, in which shops are privately owned, with a planned economy.
capitalism.basic: The lesson compared a system of privately owned shops with a planned economy.

ceremony.simple: A formal event with set actions, often to mark an important occasion.
ceremony.detailed: A structured public or private ritual — such as a citizenship event or ANZAC service — that uses words, symbols, and order to mark meaning.
ceremony.example: Families filled the hall for the citizenship ceremony, where new Australians made a pledge.
ceremony.basic: Families filled the hall for the formal event where new Australians made a pledge.

charter.simple: A formal written document that sets out rights, rules, or the aims of a group.
charter.detailed: An official founding or rights document that grants powers, lists principles, or states what an organisation or people may do.
charter.example: The student council wrote a charter that promised fair elections and an open complaints box.
charter.basic: The student council wrote a founding set of rules for fair elections.

chronology.simple: The order in which events happened, from earliest to latest.
chronology.detailed: A time sequence of events, or the study of arranging those events correctly, used in history to avoid mixing causes and later results.
chronology.example: A muddled chronology made it sound as if Federation happened before the gold rushes.
chronology.basic: A muddled time-order made it sound as if Federation happened before the gold rushes.

citizenship.simple: The legal position of belonging to a country, with rights and duties.
citizenship.detailed: The status of being a recognised member of a nation, including rights such as voting (when of age) and duties such as obeying the law.
citizenship.example: The inquiry asked what rights and responsibilities come with Australian citizenship.
citizenship.basic: The inquiry asked what rights and duties come with being an Australian citizen.

colonisation.simple: The act of one country taking control of another land and sending people to settle there.
colonisation.detailed: The process by which a foreign power occupies land, establishes settlements, and imposes its rule; in Australia this involved British settlement and the dispossession of First Nations peoples.
colonisation.example: The unit examined how colonisation changed land use and First Nations lives after 1788.
colonisation.basic: The unit examined how British settlement changed land use and First Nations lives after 1788.

commemoration.simple: An event or act that honours and remembers a person or a past event.
commemoration.detailed: A ceremony, monument, or practice designed to keep a historical event or person in public memory, such as ANZAC Day services.
commemoration.example: The school's ANZAC commemoration included a minute's silence and a wreath at the memorial.
commemoration.basic: The school's ANZAC remembrance included a minute's silence.

conquest.simple: The act of taking control of a place or people by force.
conquest.detailed: The military or political taking of territory and the people in it, often followed by new rulers, laws, and settlement.
conquest.example: The map showed borders that changed after the Spanish conquest of the Aztec empire.
conquest.basic: The map showed borders that changed after Spain took the Aztec empire by force.

convict.simple: A person found guilty of a crime and, in Australian history, often sent from Britain to a colony.
convict.detailed: A person sentenced by a court; in colonial Australia many convicts were transported from Britain and Ireland to serve their sentences as forced labour.
convict.example: A convict arriving in 1788 might spend years in chains before earning a ticket of leave.
convict.basic: A prisoner sent from Britain in 1788 might spend years in chains.

court.simple: A place and system where a judge (and sometimes a jury) hears a case and applies the law.
court.detailed: An official legal body that settles disputes, tries alleged offences, and issues judgments according to statute and common law.
court.example: The class visited the local court and watched a magistrate explain a sentencing decision.
court.basic: The class visited the local law building and watched a magistrate explain a decision.

covenant.simple: A formal, serious agreement that people or groups promise to keep.
covenant.detailed: A binding pledge or treaty, often written, that sets out duties between parties; used in law, religion, and some international agreements.
covenant.example: The two councils signed a covenant to share the river water fairly in dry years.
covenant.basic: The two councils signed a serious written promise to share the river water.

declaration.simple: An official public statement of a decision, fact, or set of rights.
declaration.detailed: A formal announcement, often written, that states a position, independence, emergency, or list of rights for the record.
declaration.example: Students compared Australia's federation documents with the American declaration of independence.
declaration.basic: Students compared Australia's federation documents with America's formal independence statement.

embassy.simple: A country's official office in another country's capital, and the people who work there.
embassy.detailed: The diplomatic mission that represents one nation in another, usually in the capital city, handling passports, talks, and official business.
embassy.example: Travellers queued at the embassy to replace passports stolen on the train.
embassy.basic: Travellers queued at Australia's official office overseas to replace stolen passports.

emigration.simple: The act of leaving your own country to live permanently in another.
emigration.detailed: Movement out of a home country to settle elsewhere; the counterpart of immigration, which is arrival in the new country.
emigration.example: Gold-rush emigration from China and Europe changed the population of several Australian colonies.
emigration.basic: People leaving China and Europe for the goldfields changed several colonies.

ethnicity.simple: A shared cultural background, language, or ancestry that a group of people identify with.
ethnicity.detailed: A social identity based on common heritage, language, customs, or origin, distinct from (though sometimes overlapping with) nationality or race.
ethnicity.example: The census question on ethnicity asked people which cultural backgrounds they identified with.
ethnicity.basic: The census asked people which cultural backgrounds they identified with.

explorer.simple: A person who travels into little-known places to map, study, or report on them.
explorer.detailed: Someone who journeys into unfamiliar territory to gather geographical, scientific, or commercial knowledge; in Australian history the term is often used for inland and coastal expeditions.
explorer.example: The diary of the explorer described waterholes that First Nations guides already knew well.
explorer.basic: The traveller's diary described waterholes that First Nations guides already knew.

governor.simple: The Crown's representative in an Australian state, or the official who once ran a colony.
governor.detailed: A vice-regal or colonial official who represents the monarch and, in earlier times, held executive power over a colony's government.
governor.example: In early New South Wales the governor could make orders that had the force of law.
governor.basic: In early New South Wales the Crown's official could make orders that had the force of law.

identity.simple: Who a person or group is, including the qualities they see as making them themselves.
identity.detailed: The sense of self or group belonging formed by culture, history, roles, and personal choices; a key idea in HASS discussions of community.
identity.example: The exhibition asked how sport, language, and Country shape Australian identity.
identity.basic: The exhibition asked how sport, language, and Country shape who Australians feel they are.

ideology.simple: A set of ideas that a group uses to explain how society should work.
ideology.detailed: A fairly organised system of political or social beliefs that shapes policies, slogans, and the way supporters interpret events.
ideology.example: The article said the party's ideology favoured smaller government and lower taxes.
ideology.basic: The article said the party's set of beliefs favoured smaller government.

independence.simple: The state of being free from another country's rule or from someone else's control.
independence.detailed: Political self-rule, or personal autonomy, in which a nation or person makes decisions without being governed by an outside power.
independence.example: India gained independence from British rule in 1947 after a long campaign.
independence.basic: India became free from British rule in 1947.

industrialisation.simple: The change from making most goods by hand to making them in factories with machines.
industrialisation.detailed: The historical process in which an economy shifts toward large-scale factory production, powered machinery, and urban wage labour.
industrialisation.example: Industrialisation in nineteenth-century Britain pulled many families from farms into crowded mill towns.
industrialisation.basic: The rise of factories in nineteenth-century Britain pulled many families into mill towns.

inequality.simple: An unfair difference in wealth, rights, or chances between people or groups.
inequality.detailed: A patterned gap in income, power, health, or opportunity that leaves some people systematically worse off than others.
inequality.example: The graph of income inequality showed the top tenth earning far more than the bottom tenth.
inequality.basic: The graph showed a big unfair gap between the highest and lowest earners.

inflation.simple: A general rise in prices, so the same money buys less than before.
inflation.detailed: A sustained increase in the average price level of goods and services, which reduces the purchasing power of a currency.
inflation.example: When inflation rose, the same lunch money bought a smaller sandwich than last year.
inflation.basic: When prices rose across the board, the same lunch money bought a smaller sandwich.

institution.simple: An established organisation or long-lasting custom that helps a society run, such as a court, school, or parliament.
institution.detailed: A durable public or social structure — a body, rule system, or tradition — that organises behaviour over time, from hospitals to the idea of marriage.
institution.example: Parliament is an institution that makes laws, not just a building on the hill in Canberra.
institution.basic: Parliament is an established public body that makes laws.

invasion.simple: The act of entering a country or land with force in order to take control.
invasion.detailed: A hostile entry of armed forces, or a sudden overwhelming arrival, that aims to occupy territory or defeat the people already there.
invasion.example: Some historians describe 1788 as an invasion because the First Fleet arrived without First Nations consent.
invasion.basic: Some historians say 1788 was a forced entry because the First Fleet arrived without consent.

jury.simple: A group of ordinary citizens who listen to a trial and decide whether the accused is guilty.
jury.detailed: A panel of eligible citizens sworn to hear evidence in court and deliver a verdict, a key feature of many common-law criminal trials.
jury.example: The jury left the courtroom to discuss the evidence in private before giving a verdict.
jury.basic: The group of ordinary citizens left to discuss the evidence in private.

legislature.simple: The group of elected people who make and change the laws.
legislature.detailed: The law-making branch of government, such as the Australian Parliament or a state parliament, as distinct from the courts and the ministry.
legislature.example: A bill does not become law until the legislature has debated and passed it.
legislature.basic: A bill does not become law until the law-making body has debated and passed it.

liberty.simple: The freedom to live, speak, and act without unfair control.
liberty.detailed: The condition of being free from arbitrary power, including civil liberties such as speech, movement, and a fair trial.
liberty.example: The speaker said liberty includes the right to criticise the government without fear.
liberty.basic: The speaker said freedom includes the right to criticise the government without fear.

literacy.simple: The ability to read and write well enough to use texts in everyday life.
literacy.detailed: Skill in reading, writing, and, in modern classrooms, interpreting a range of texts so a person can learn, work, and take part in civic life.
literacy.example: The library programme aimed to lift literacy so every girl could tackle a scholarship paper.
literacy.basic: The library programme aimed to lift reading and writing so every girl could tackle a hard paper.

majority.simple: More than half of a group, or the larger part of it.
majority.detailed: A number of votes or people greater than 50 per cent, or the larger share of a population; in parliament it often means enough seats to form government.
majority.example: A majority of the class voted for a longer inquiry, so the teacher changed the timetable.
majority.basic: More than half the class voted for a longer inquiry.

manufacturing.simple: The business of making goods in factories, rather than growing them or selling services.
manufacturing.detailed: The industrial production of articles from raw materials or parts, typically on a large scale, as opposed to farming or office work.
manufacturing.example: Car manufacturing in that city shrank when the last assembly plant closed.
manufacturing.basic: Factory car-making in that city shrank when the last plant closed.

maritime.simple: Relating to the sea, ships, and sea trade.
maritime.detailed: Of or connected with navigation, shipping, ports, and the law or history of the sea, as in a seafaring museum or a sea boundary.
maritime.example: The maritime museum displayed the compass from a wool clipper that once left Sydney.
maritime.basic: The sea-trade museum displayed the compass from a wool clipper.

memorial.simple: A statue, building, or plaque set up to honour people or an event from the past.
memorial.detailed: A physical or ceremonial reminder — monument, park, or service — created so a community does not forget the dead or a significant event.
memorial.example: Names of local soldiers are carved on the sandstone memorial in the main street.
memorial.basic: Names of local soldiers are carved on the sandstone monument in the main street.

merchant.simple: A person whose work is buying and selling goods, especially in large amounts or across seas.
merchant.detailed: A trader who purchases commodities to sell at a profit, historically including ship-owning merchants who linked ports and colonies.
merchant.example: The merchant imported tea and exported wool through the busy Sydney docks.
merchant.basic: The trader imported tea and exported wool through the Sydney docks.

minority.simple: A smaller part of a group, or a group of people who are fewer than the rest in a community.
minority.detailed: Less than half of a set of votes or people; also a community whose culture, language, or identity differs from the larger surrounding population.
minority.example: Being in a minority on the council did not stop her from asking hard questions.
minority.basic: Being in the smaller group on the council did not stop her from asking hard questions.

monarchy.simple: A system of government with a king, queen, or other hereditary ruler.
monarchy.detailed: A form of state in which a monarch is head of state, either ruling with real power or, as in Australia, serving as a constitutional figure represented by a governor-general.
monarchy.example: Australia is a constitutional monarchy: the King is head of state, but elected ministers run the government.
monarchy.basic: Australia has a king as head of state, but elected ministers run the government.

multiculturalism.simple: The idea that many cultures can live together in one country and be respected.
multiculturalism.detailed: A social policy and attitude that recognises and supports cultural diversity within a nation, rather than demanding that everyone follow one culture only.
multiculturalism.example: Harmony Day lessons presented multiculturalism as a strength of modern Australian suburbs.
multiculturalism.basic: Harmony Day lessons presented living with many cultures as a strength of Australian suburbs.

nationalism.simple: A strong belief that your nation is especially important and should be independent or put first.
nationalism.detailed: A political feeling or movement that emphasises national identity, unity, and often superiority or self-rule, which can inspire both independence campaigns and conflict.
nationalism.example: Nineteenth-century nationalism helped some European peoples demand their own countries.
nationalism.basic: Nineteenth-century national pride helped some European peoples demand their own countries.

negotiation.simple: Talking with the other side to try to reach an agreement.
negotiation.detailed: A structured discussion in which parties bargain, compromise, and set terms, used in diplomacy, industrial disputes, and everyday problem-solving.
negotiation.example: After a long negotiation the two councils agreed to share the cost of the new bridge.
negotiation.basic: After a long set of talks the two councils agreed to share the cost of the bridge.

opposition.simple: The people or party that disagree with those in power, or the act of resisting a plan.
opposition.detailed: In parliament, the parties not in government who scrutinise ministers; more generally, organised resistance to a policy, idea, or group.
opposition.example: The opposition questioned the premier about hospital waiting times at question time.
opposition.basic: The rival party questioned the premier about hospital waiting times.

outback.simple: The remote inland parts of Australia, far from the big coastal cities.
outback.detailed: The sparsely populated, often arid interior of Australia, away from the densely settled coast, used in geography and national imagery.
outback.example: The documentary followed a Flying Doctor flight to an outback clinic 400 kilometres from the nearest city.
outback.basic: The documentary followed a Flying Doctor flight to a remote inland clinic.

pioneer.simple: One of the first people to settle, try, or develop something new.
pioneer.detailed: A person who opens the way for others, whether by settling new land, inventing a method, or being first in a field of work.
pioneer.example: She was a pioneer of girls' cricket in the district and later coached the state side.
pioneer.basic: She was one of the first to build girls' cricket in the district.

politician.simple: A person whose job is to work in government or to seek election to public office.
politician.detailed: Someone who holds or campaigns for political office, making or influencing laws and public decisions, for example a member of parliament.
politician.example: The local politician visited the school to hear students' questions about the new bus route.
politician.basic: The elected local member visited the school to hear questions about the bus route.

poverty.simple: The state of being very poor and lacking money for basic needs.
poverty.detailed: A condition in which people cannot afford adequate food, housing, health care, or schooling, measured in absolute or relative terms.
poverty.example: The charity report linked child poverty to crowded housing and missed school meals.
poverty.basic: The charity report linked being very poor to crowded housing and missed meals.

premier.simple: The elected leader of an Australian state government.
premier.detailed: The head of government in an Australian state, usually the leader of the party that holds a majority in the lower house.
premier.example: The Victorian premier announced extra trains after the inquiry into overcrowding.
premier.basic: Victoria's state leader announced extra trains after the inquiry.

privilege.simple: A special right or advantage that only some people have.
privilege.detailed: An unearned or extra benefit attached to a role, class, or group, which can make life easier than it is for people without that advantage.
privilege.example: Reserved seats at the front were a privilege for students who had volunteered all term.
privilege.basic: Reserved seats at the front were a special advantage for the volunteers.

proclamation.simple: An official public announcement, often made by a government or a monarch.
proclamation.detailed: A formal published notice that declares a law, emergency, holiday, or new status so that the public is taken to know it.
proclamation.example: A colonial proclamation claimed land that First Nations nations had never ceded.
proclamation.basic: A colonial public notice claimed land that First Nations nations had never given up.

propaganda.simple: Information spread to make people accept a particular view, often by hiding the other side.
propaganda.detailed: Persuasive material, sometimes misleading, produced by a government or group to shape public opinion rather than to present balanced evidence.
propaganda.example: The wartime poster was propaganda: it showed only heroic soldiers and none of the costs of battle.
propaganda.basic: The wartime poster was one-sided advertising for the war.

prosperity.simple: A time or condition of being successful and having enough money and resources.
prosperity.detailed: Sustained economic well-being for a person, community, or nation, marked by employment, rising living standards, and confidence.
prosperity.example: The gold rush brought sudden prosperity to some towns and left others empty when the gold ran out.
prosperity.basic: The gold rush brought sudden wealth to some towns.

rebellion.simple: An organised fight or uprising against the people in power.
rebellion.detailed: Open, collective resistance to authority, ranging from a protest that turns into revolt to an armed attempt to overthrow rulers.
rebellion.example: The Eureka rebellion began as a protest by miners against a harsh licence fee.
rebellion.basic: The Eureka uprising began as a protest by miners against a harsh licence fee.

reform.simple: A change made to improve a law, system, or practice.
reform.detailed: A deliberate improvement to institutions or rules, intended to correct injustice or inefficiency without necessarily overthrowing the whole system.
reform.example: Voting reform in the 1890s extended the ballot to more adults in some Australian colonies.
reform.basic: Changes to voting rules in the 1890s let more adults vote in some colonies.

refugee.simple: A person who has fled their country because of war, danger, or persecution.
refugee.detailed: Someone who cannot safely return home and seeks protection in another country because of a well-founded fear of harm.
refugee.example: The class interview with a refugee focused on the journey, not just on the war they had left.
refugee.basic: The class interview with someone who had fled danger focused on the journey.

republic.simple: A country whose head of state is elected or chosen, not a king or queen.
republic.detailed: A form of government in which political power rests with the people or their representatives and the head of state is not a hereditary monarch.
republic.example: Some Australians argue the nation should become a republic with an Australian head of state.
republic.basic: Some Australians argue the nation should have an elected head of state instead of a king.

revolution.simple: A sudden, far-reaching change in government or society, often after a popular uprising.
revolution.detailed: A fundamental overthrow or transformation of a political or social order, as in France in 1789 or the later factory-age upheaval.
revolution.example: The industrial revolution changed how cloth was made, but it was not a single street battle.
revolution.basic: The great factory change of the 1700s changed how cloth was made.

slavery.simple: The system of owning people as property and forcing them to work without freedom or pay.
slavery.detailed: An institution in which human beings are treated as property, denied legal personhood, and compelled to labour for the benefit of owners.
slavery.example: The inquiry contrasted chattel slavery with other forms of forced labour in the Pacific.
slavery.basic: The inquiry contrasted owning people as property with other forms of forced labour.

suburb.simple: A mainly residential area on the edge of a city, away from the crowded centre.
suburb.detailed: An urban district, often of houses and local shops, that forms part of a larger city but sits outside the central business area.
suburb.example: A new railway station can turn a quiet suburb into a busy place to live and shop.
suburb.basic: A new railway station can turn a quiet outer neighbourhood into a busy place.

taxation.simple: The system of collecting money from people and businesses to pay for public services.
taxation.detailed: The legal raising of revenue by government through taxes on income, goods, or property, used to fund schools, hospitals, and other services.
taxation.example: The HASS debate asked whether taxation should rise to pay for flood-proof roads.
taxation.basic: The debate asked whether taxes should rise to pay for flood-proof roads.

territory.simple: An area of land under the control of a government, or a region that is not yet a full state.
territory.detailed: A defined area of land (and sometimes sea) over which a state claims authority; in Australia the word also names regions that are not full states.
territory.example: The Northern Territory is a territory, not a state, so the federal parliament can still override some of its laws.
territory.basic: The Northern Territory is a region that is not a full state.

tourism.simple: The business of people travelling for holidays and the services that support those visits.
tourism.detailed: The industry and activity of visitors travelling for leisure or interest, including transport, accommodation, and the effects on local places.
tourism.example: Reef tourism brings money to the town, but too many boats can damage the coral.
tourism.basic: Holiday visits to the reef bring money, but too many boats can damage the coral.

unemployment.simple: The situation of people who want paid work but cannot find a job.
unemployment.detailed: The condition, and the official rate, of people in the labour force who are without work and actively seeking it.
unemployment.example: Youth unemployment rose in the town when the cannery closed before Christmas.
unemployment.basic: The number of young people without jobs rose when the cannery closed.

urbanisation.simple: The process of more people living in towns and cities instead of in the countryside.
urbanisation.detailed: The growth in the proportion of a population that lives in urban areas, often accompanied by expanding suburbs and changing land use.
urbanisation.example: Urbanisation along the coast has turned market gardens into streets of new houses.
urbanisation.basic: The spread of cities along the coast has turned market gardens into streets of houses.

voyage.simple: A long journey, especially by sea or through space.
voyage.detailed: An extended passage by ship (or spacecraft), often used for exploration, migration, or trade rather than a short local trip.
voyage.example: The First Fleet's voyage from England to Botany Bay lasted more than eight months.
voyage.basic: The First Fleet's long sea journey from England to Botany Bay lasted more than eight months.

welfare.simple: Help that a government or group gives people in need, or a person's general well-being.
welfare.detailed: Public support such as payments, housing, or services for people who are sick, unemployed, or poor; also used more broadly for health and happiness.
welfare.example: The inquiry asked whether welfare payments were enough for a family after a flood.
welfare.basic: The inquiry asked whether government help was enough for a family after a flood.

workforce.simple: All the people who are available to do paid work in a country, industry, or company.
workforce.detailed: The collective body of employees and job-seekers in an economy or organisation, sometimes analysed by skill, age, or industry.
workforce.example: A shortage in the teaching workforce meant some classes were split between two rooms.
workforce.basic: A shortage of available teachers meant some classes were split between two rooms.

alliteration.simple: Repeating the same starting sound in nearby words, as in 'wild, wet weather'.
alliteration.detailed: A sound device in which the same consonant (or sometimes vowel) sound begins closely placed words, used to make a phrase memorable or musical.
alliteration.example: The headline 'Fierce flames flatten farmland' used alliteration to make the disaster sound sudden.
alliteration.basic: The headline repeated the 'f' sound to make the disaster sound sudden.

autobiography.simple: A book in which a person tells the story of their own life.
autobiography.detailed: A non-fiction narrative written by the subject about their own experiences, as distinct from a biography written by someone else.
autobiography.example: In her autobiography the scientist described the shed where she first grew crystals.
autobiography.basic: In her own life story the scientist described the shed where she first grew crystals.

ballad.simple: A poem or song that tells a story, often in short verses with a strong beat.
ballad.detailed: A narrative poem or song, traditionally in simple stanzas with refrain or rhyme, used for folk tales, love stories, and dramatic events.
ballad.example: The bush ballad told of a rider who vanished in a dust storm on the plains.
ballad.basic: The bush story-song told of a rider who vanished in a dust storm.

characterisation.simple: The way a writer shows what a character is like through actions, speech, and description.
characterisation.detailed: The techniques an author uses to construct a character — direct description, dialogue, thoughts, and other people's reactions — so the reader can infer traits.
characterisation.example: The characterisation of the captain relied on short orders rather than long speeches about bravery.
characterisation.basic: The writer showed the captain mainly through short orders, not speeches about bravery.

comedy.simple: A play, film, or story meant to amuse, usually ending more happily than a tragedy.
comedy.detailed: A dramatic or narrative genre that uses humour, mistaken identity, or playful conflict and typically restores order or marriage rather than disaster.
comedy.example: Their class comedy ended with the lost dog and the mayor arriving on stage at the same moment.
comedy.basic: Their funny class play ended with the lost dog and the mayor arriving together.

couplet.simple: Two lines of poetry that sit together and often rhyme.
couplet.detailed: A pair of successive verse lines, frequently rhymed and of similar length, used to close a sonnet or to drive a ballad forward.
couplet.example: She finished the poem with a couplet that snapped the riddle shut in two rhyming lines.
couplet.basic: She finished the poem with two rhyming lines that snapped the riddle shut.

dialect.simple: A form of a language used by people from a particular place or group.
dialect.detailed: A regional or social variety of a language, with its own vocabulary, grammar, or pronunciation, as distinct from the standard classroom form.
dialect.example: The narrator's Queensland dialect used 'arvo' and 'yeah-nah' that a London reader might need glossed.
dialect.basic: The narrator's Queensland way of speaking used 'arvo' and 'yeah-nah'.

drama.simple: A story written to be performed by actors, or writing that feels tense and emotional.
drama.detailed: A genre meant for stage or screen performance; also used more loosely for serious conflict in a narrative that holds an audience.
drama.example: In drama they blocked the scene so the argument happened downstage, closer to the audience.
drama.basic: In the play lesson they placed the argument closer to the audience.

epilogue.simple: A short section at the end of a book or play that tells what happens afterwards.
epilogue.detailed: A closing speech or chapter after the main action, used to settle remaining questions or show characters at a later time.
epilogue.example: The epilogue jumped forward ten years and showed the twins still arguing on the same jetty.
epilogue.basic: The last extra chapter jumped forward ten years and showed the twins still arguing.

fable.simple: A short story, often with animals as characters, that teaches a moral lesson.
fable.detailed: A brief allegorical tale, traditionally ending with an explicit moral, in which animals or objects behave like people to criticise human faults.
fable.example: In the fable the proud magpie lost its berries because it would not share the branch.
fable.basic: In the short moral story the proud magpie lost its berries.

flashback.simple: A scene that jumps back to an earlier time in the story.
flashback.detailed: A narrative interruption that presents events from the past so the reader understands a character's motive or a secret already in place.
flashback.example: A flashback to the flood explained why the grandmother still packed a radio in every picnic basket.
flashback.basic: A jump back to the flood explained why the grandmother still packed a radio.

folklore.simple: The traditional stories, sayings, and customs passed down in a community.
folklore.detailed: The body of legends, songs, beliefs, and practices shared by a people, usually by word of mouth rather than by a single known author.
folklore.example: Bunyip tales and bush ballads both sit in Australian folklore, though one tradition is far older.
folklore.basic: Those traditional stories and songs both sit in Australia's passed-down lore.

foreshadow.simple: To drop a hint that something will happen later in a story.
foreshadow.detailed: To plant clues — an image, a remark, or a small event — that prepare the reader for a later turning point without stating it outright.
foreshadow.example: Dark clouds in chapter one foreshadow the storm that will trap the hikers.
foreshadow.basic: Dark clouds in chapter one hint at the storm that will trap the hikers.

idiom.simple: A phrase whose meaning is not obvious from the separate words, such as 'raining cats and dogs'.
idiom.detailed: A fixed expression whose overall sense cannot be guessed by translating each word, so readers must learn it as a chunk.
idiom.example: The idiom 'kick the bucket' does not involve a real bucket; it means to die.
idiom.basic: The set phrase 'kick the bucket' does not involve a real bucket.

legend.simple: A traditional story that may be based on a real person or event but has grown more extraordinary over time.
legend.detailed: A narrative from the past that a community treats as meaningful history, even when details have been enlarged, as distinct from a myth about gods or origins.
legend.example: The legend of Ned Kelly mixes court records with stories that grew after the siege.
legend.basic: The traditional tale of Ned Kelly mixes court records with later stories.

lyric.simple: The words of a song, or a short poem that expresses feelings rather than telling a long story.
lyric.detailed: A short, song-like poem that presents a speaker's emotion or thought; also the text sung to a melody.
lyric.example: The lyric of the protest song named the river but never named the company.
lyric.basic: The words of the protest song named the river but never named the company.

myth.simple: A traditional story, often about gods or how the world began, that a culture uses to explain beliefs.
myth.detailed: A sacred or foundational narrative that explains origins, values, or natural features; different from a legend tied to a later historical figure.
myth.example: The Greek myth of Persephone was used to explain why winter returns each year.
myth.basic: The Greek origin story of Persephone was used to explain winter.

onomatopoeia.simple: A word that imitates a sound, such as 'buzz', 'crash', or 'drip'.
onomatopoeia.detailed: A sound device in which a word's pronunciation suggests the noise it names, used to make description more vivid.
onomatopoeia.example: The line 'the creek went slosh, slosh' used onomatopoeia so you could hear the boots.
onomatopoeia.basic: The line 'the creek went slosh, slosh' copied the sound of the boots.

personification.simple: Giving human qualities to an object, animal, or idea, as if it could think or speak.
personification.detailed: A figurative device that attributes human actions, feelings, or voice to something non-human in order to create mood or meaning.
personification.example: The sentence 'the drought licked the dams dry' used personification to make the weather seem greedy.
personification.basic: The sentence gave the drought a human action — licking — to make it seem greedy.

poetry.simple: Writing arranged in lines that uses sound, image, and rhythm more tightly than ordinary prose.
poetry.detailed: A literary form that shapes language into lines and stanzas, relying on sound devices, imagery, and compressed meaning rather than only on plot.
poetry.example: In the poetry unit Oliver had to mark the stressed beats, not just retell the story.
poetry.basic: In the poems unit Oliver had to mark the stressed beats.

prologue.simple: A short opening section that comes before the main story or play.
prologue.detailed: An introductory chapter, speech, or scene that sets context, introduces a narrator, or shows an event that happens before the main action.
prologue.example: The prologue showed the fire before chapter one began with the rebuilt street.
prologue.basic: The opening extra scene showed the fire before chapter one began.

rhyme.simple: When words share the same ending sound, such as 'night' and 'light'.
rhyme.detailed: A sound pattern in which the final stressed vowels and following sounds of words match, used in verse, song, and some rhetoric.
rhyme.example: He changed 'road' to 'track' so the last line would rhyme with 'back'.
rhyme.basic: He changed 'road' to 'track' so the last line would share an ending sound with 'back'.

rhythm.simple: The pattern of beats or stresses that you can hear in music, poetry, or a sentence.
rhythm.detailed: The regular or varied recurrence of stressed and unstressed sounds that gives verse, prose, or music its pulse.
rhythm.example: Clapping the rhythm showed that the bush poem used a steady four-beat line.
rhythm.basic: Clapping the beat showed that the bush poem used a steady four-beat line.

sonnet.simple: A fourteen-line poem with a set rhyme pattern, often about love or a big idea.
sonnet.detailed: A short lyric of fourteen lines, classically in iambic pentameter, with a recognised rhyme scheme such as Shakespearean or Petrarchan.
sonnet.example: Her sonnet turned at line nine, when the drought image became a promise of rain.
sonnet.basic: Her fourteen-line poem turned at line nine, when the drought image became rain.

stanza.simple: A grouped set of lines in a poem, like a paragraph of verse.
stanza.detailed: A unit of a poem set off by a space, with a recurring number of lines and often a repeating rhyme or rhythm pattern.
stanza.example: Each stanza of the ballad ended with the same refrain about the dry creek.
stanza.basic: Each grouped set of lines ended with the same refrain about the dry creek.

stereotype.simple: An over-simple, fixed idea about a whole group of people that ignores individual differences.
stereotype.detailed: A widely held but reductive image or assumption that treats members of a group as if they were all the same, often unfairly.
stereotype.example: The novel challenged the stereotype that every scientist is a quiet man in a white coat.
stereotype.basic: The novel challenged the lazy idea that every scientist is a quiet man in a white coat.

subplot.simple: A smaller story that runs alongside the main plot.
subplot.detailed: A secondary storyline that involves supporting characters or a lesser conflict and usually connects thematically to the main action.
subplot.example: The subplot about the missing bicycle mirrored the larger mystery of the vanished map.
subplot.basic: The smaller side-story about the missing bicycle mirrored the larger mystery.

suspense.simple: The tense feeling of not knowing what will happen next.
suspense.detailed: A narrative effect that delays key information or outcome so the reader feels anxiety, curiosity, or dread while waiting.
suspense.example: Leaving the torch battery untested built suspense before the cave scene.
suspense.basic: Leaving the torch battery untested made readers tense before the cave scene.

tragedy.simple: A serious play or story in which the main character suffers a disastrous end.
tragedy.detailed: A dramatic genre that presents a fall from fortune, often through a character flaw or cruel fate, and aims to stir pity and fear rather than laughter.
tragedy.example: In the Greek tragedy the king learns the truth only after the damage cannot be undone.
tragedy.basic: In the serious Greek play the king learns the truth too late.

verse.simple: Writing in lines of poetry, or one such line or section.
verse.detailed: Language organised as poetry rather than prose; also a single metrical line, or a numbered section of a song or poem.
verse.example: The hymn's second verse named the river that ran behind the old church.
verse.basic: The hymn's second section named the river behind the old church.

voice.simple: The distinctive way a narrator or writer sounds on the page.
voice.detailed: The personality, attitude, and style that come through in a text — first-person, formal, wry, and so on — as if a particular speaker were talking.
voice.example: The diary voice was chatty and misspelt, which made the fear in chapter five more shocking.
voice.basic: The diary sounded chatty and misspelt, which made the fear in chapter five more shocking.

annotate.simple: To add short notes to a text as you read, explaining or marking important parts.
annotate.detailed: To write comments, questions, or labels on or beside a passage so the reader records thinking, sources, or key ideas for later use.
annotate.example: Oliver had to annotate the article in the margin, not just highlight whole paragraphs yellow.
annotate.basic: Oliver had to add short notes to the article, not just highlight it yellow.

brainstorm.simple: To list many ideas quickly, without judging them yet.
brainstorm.detailed: To generate a wide set of possibilities in a short burst, delaying criticism so unusual or useful ideas are not shut down too early.
brainstorm.example: They had five minutes to brainstorm titles before anyone was allowed to say 'that's silly'.
brainstorm.basic: They had five minutes to list titles before anyone was allowed to judge them.

cross-check.simple: To check a fact by comparing it with a second, independent source.
cross-check.detailed: To verify information by matching it against another account, data set, or method so a single error is less likely to stand.
cross-check.example: Always cross-check a surprising statistic with the original table, not just a social-media post.
cross-check.basic: Always check a surprising statistic against the original table as well.

double-check.simple: To check something a second time so a mistake is less likely.
double-check.detailed: To repeat a calculation, spelling, or instruction in order to catch slips before work is submitted or equipment is used.
